correctness.rationale: The coordinate inequalities give \(\|K^*x\|^2=|x_1|^2\le\sum|\langle x,f_n\rangle|^2\le\|x\|^2\), so \(F\) is a \(K\)-frame, while the scaling produces the canonical orthonormal basis. Since \(R(T_F)=D(D_a)\) and \(D_aT_F=I\), the composition is bounded, but for \(y_m=e_m/m\) the ratio \(\|D_ay_m\|/\|y_m\|=m\) is unbounded. The general equivalence follows because a Bessel scaled family has analysis operator \(A\), and Douglas converts its lower \(K\)-frame inequality to \(R(K)\subset R(A^*)\). If \(R(T_F)\) is closed, the bounded Moore–Penrose inverse on \(\ker(T_F)^\perp\) gives \(D_a|_{R(T_F)}=T_GT_F^\dagger\). Fresh coordinate checks reproduced the unbounded ratio for arbitrary tested coordinates.

final_claim: A rank-one closed-range \(K\) and the \(K\)-frame \(f_1=e_1,\ f_n=e_n/n\) admit the unbounded scaling \(a_1=1,\ a_n=n\) to the orthonormal basis, so boundedness of \(D_a\) on \(R(T_F)\) is not necessary for the scaled family to be a \(K\)-frame. In general the exact criterion is \(R(T_F)\subset D(D_a)\), boundedness of \(A=D_aT_F\), and \(R(K)\subset R(A^*)\); if \(R(T_F)\) is closed then the disputed range-boundedness conclusion does hold.
